title: Deduplicating 7 million records in two minutes with Splink | by Robin Linacre | Data Science Collective | Medium
description: Deduplicating 7 million records in two minutes with Splink | by Robin Linacre | Data Science Collective | Medium # Deduplicating 7 million records in two minutes with Splink ## Super fast entity resolution within messy data using DuckDB ... Feb 12, 2025 ... Data deduplication is the problem of matching entities across multiple records: ... Splink is a free, open source Python library to address this problem. This post demonstrates one of its key features: It is very fast. It presents results from benchmarking Splink on a 7 million row dataset, using the default DuckDB backend. ... To the best of my knowledge, these results show that it is the fastest free tool for accurately deduplicating large datasets â by at least an order of magnitude. ... To test the performance of Splink, a dataset of people was collected from the Wikidata Query Service. ... ### The Splink code The full Splink script is included as an appendex to this post. The script is intended to be representative of a real-life large scale linking job: - It uses a variety of complex fuzzy comparisons to detect similarity between records (e.g. Josef vs Joseph or 1845â01â01 vs 1845â01â13) - The script accounts not just for differences in string variables, but models geographical distance between birth locations - It uses term frequency adjustments to ensure matches different names are scored differently (e.g. a match on John is weighted lower than a match on Lucas) For the purpose of this post, I chose to make a relatively large number of comparisons per input record (around 100) to demonstrate the speed of Splink. That means the linkage job evaluates over 1 billion pairwise record comparisons. In real record linkage scenarios, especially those where we have more columns of data about the entities, itâs often possible to use tighter blocking rules, resulting in fewer record comparisons per input record. ... The following chart shows runtimes broken down by the type of workloads (estimating model parameters, predicting matching pairs, clustering matched pairs into entities using graph algorithms): ... The workload parallelises extremely well, with much shorter runtimes on larger matchines. We can also see that even on a laptop-spec machine (c6g.2xlarge = 8vCPU/16Gb RAM) the longest operation (predict) takes only around 16 minutes. ### Comparisons to other libraries A chart of the runtimes of three other popular open source record linkage packages can be found in a paper accompanying the fastLink R package: ... The chart shows that of the three, fastLink has by far the best performance, at 400 minutes to deduplicate 300,000 records on an 8 core machine, with runtime increasing approximately quadratically with the number of input records. Splink is able to deduplicate the same number of records in less than a minute on a comparable machine, suggesting itâs at least two orders of magnitude faster. ... This post considers ... only. Accuracy statistics would only be valid on the specific dataset used for benchmarking, and I do not have comparative accuracy statistics for other libraries. However, an independent empirical study has found Splinkâs accuracy compares favourably to alternatives. There are also theoretical reasons to believe other methodologies are unlikely to be significantly more accurate. ... ### Appendix: Full Splink Script ``` import pandas as pdfrom splink.duckdb.blocking_rule_library import block_onfrom splink.duckdb.comparison_library import (    distance_in_km_at_thresholds,    exact_match,    jaro_winkler_at_thresholds,    levenshtein_at_thresholds,)from splink.duckdb.linker import DuckDBLinkerdf = pd.read_parquet("7m_prepareed.parquet")splink_settings = {    "link_type": "dedupe_only", And then came the realization: this was not just her problem. If she was facing it, others were too. And they deserved a solution. ... ## Why Identity Resolution Still ... What is fascinating is not that identity resolution is rare, it is that despite its rarity, it is central to almost every serious data initiative. Marketing teams need it for 360-degree customer views. Risk and compliance teams need it for watchlist deduplication and fraud detection. Governments and non-profits need it for program eligibility, household-based targeting, or population deduplication. And yet, many still attempt to hand-code heuristics or manually match entities in spreadsheets or data frames. That is not sustainable. The problem is too complex, too large-scale, and too foundational to keep solving in ad hoc ways. ... Out of these: only 11 repositories focus on identity resolution. Just 172 touch on entity resolution. 322 explore fuzzy matching. 457 cover deduplication. 17 mention customer data platforms. And 26 address master data management. ... For a problem ... foundational, connecting ... few have taken it on ... solve it themselves ... Zingg is not just a tool. It is the result of years of direct experience with the edge cases, the false matches, the scale bottlenecks, and the architectural decisions no one talks about. We built algorithms that can handle uncertainty, sparsity, and duplication and continuously learn from feedback. We built for datasets with millions of rows. We built for teams who do not want to label data just to get started. And we built with love because we knew how frustrating this problem could be when you are facing it alone. ... If you are a data engineer stuck stitching together fragmented records, a CTO wondering why your customer data still is not unified, or a team lead trying to resolve people, suppliers, or products across platforms, we see you. You could build your own identity resolution pipeline. Many have. But it takes time. It takes experimentation. And it takes living this problem, not just coding for it. That is why we built Zingg. For marketing, it powers your composable CDP, helping you finally unify that elusive customer view. For procurement, it lets you understand your suppliers better, and track who you are really doing business with. For compliance, it strengthens your response to CCPA, GDPR, KYC, and AML mandates, by starting with clean, resolved data. ... title: Deduplicating Records: Is Machine Learning the Answer?
description: Entity Resolution May 8, 2025 Real-world data is far from perfect. When we enter data into a system, like a Salesforce CRM, chances are that a copy of that record exists already. These duplicates need to be removed so that our sales and marketing can work efficiently and effectively. More than a single record for a customer in the CRM hurts our outreach. Identifying duplicate records with variations and retaining a single copy of them is known as deduplication. Deduplication is a critical step in data cleansing and involves the same entity being represented in slightly different ways. This entity could be anything an organization has a relationship with customer, location, supplier, partner. There could be minor typographical errors in some of the fields, middle initials or names present or absent, differing ordering of words, presence of suffixes and prefixes. There could be missing fields altogether. When records are referring to the same real-world entity, they need to be identified as duplicates even with all these differences between their attributes. ... each sourced from a different database. ... present in one file and missing in another. A typical customer record will have a name and address and sometimes an email address or phone number. Customer Names could be further separated in first and last name, initial, title, etc, all of which could be either in a field of its own or concatenated and put together in the same field. Customer data cleansing relies heavily on deduplicating such customer records to ensure that a single copy of the customer is accessed and utilized. ... A trained human can handle all these differences as long as the data is small, but as record sizes increase, it is not possible to do customer deduplication or address deduplication manually. Due to subtle differences between attributes and lack of a common identifier among the records, coding rules for customer matching or address matching for deduplication is difficult. What if we could apply machine learning to find patterns for duplicates in the different datasets? Patterns about variations? Patterns about extraneous characters? Patterns about missing fields? If we could use machine learning for deduplication, there would be no need to define complex rules or algorithms for matching fields. We would no longer worry about thresholds for similarity. Training to learn the deduplication and matching rules with a simple yes and no about matches and non-matches would do the trick. Once trained, the machine learning models could easily remove duplicates in customers, addresses, and suppliers so as to create a clean and comprehensive list of customers and suppliers. One would not have to ever worry about messy unclean data in CRM and other systems. Zingg Labs ... Lewes, Delaware 19958 United States
